title: Measuring AI code assistants and agents with the AI Measurement Framework
summary: DX founders present an AI measurement framework (utilization, impact, cost), warning against acceptance-rate metrics and self-reported speedups and urging baselines.

assertions.quote: acceptance rate is an incredibly flawed and inaccurate metric because when developers accept code, much of that code is often then later modified or deleted

verdicts.note: Accepted suggestions are often later rewritten or deleted, and output volume has long been a poor proxy for productivity; controlled studies measure task time or delivery instead.
METR 2025 argues that lines of code and task counts can rise without productivity (more verbose code, PRs split up), and so uses fixed, pre-defined tasks with time to completion as the outcome.

Authors argue acceptance rate and immediate correctness capture only what happens at introduction and miss later maintenance, where 22.7% of AI-introduced issues persist; they also cite work finding acceptance rate correlates with self-reported productivity.

Authors state completion acceptance rates are 'far from' the maintainability and productivity constructs, and deliberately exclude studies relying on acceptance rate, keystrokes or LoC; assertion, not test.

Google: the share of committed AI code is a good proxy for time savings in most cases, but it misses value such as an imperfect first draft that locates the change sites, so they judge success by end-to-end time saved instead.

assertions.quote: combining both self-reported data with telemetry and systems data is the way to go as always.

verdicts.note: Self-reports alone overstate speedups (METR) and telemetry alone misses experience and quality, so triangulating against a baseline is standard measurement practice.

Anthropic pairs surveys with 200K Claude Code transcripts and says self-reports (subject to social-desirability and recall bias) should be read alongside objective usage data, with better instruments needed.

assertions.quote: developers uh self- reports of the fact that they were faster with AI than without it were were actually wrong in in many cases

verdicts.note: METR found devs believed they were ~20% faster while measured slower; other studies also show self-reports outrunning measured gains.

assertions.quote: we do see not in all cases but in many cases a decrease in code self-reported co code maintainability scores.

verdicts.note: Vendor survey data shows some decline, but the Echoes of AI controlled study found no significant maintainability penalty, so the effect is uncertain.
In a 272-developer follow-up using multi-item self-report scales, AI use was associated with lower code maintainability and more technical debt. This held after dropping zero-experience respondents.

assertions.quote: giving designers and PMs some of these vibe coding tools as a way to do more rapid prototyping and exploration.

verdicts.note: Tools like Lovable, v0, Replit let non-developers produce working prototypes; widely observed.

assertions.quote: the key would be to have that code go through the same code reviews, the same gating quality processes as any other code

verdicts.note: Given documented defect and security rates in AI code, human review before merge is standard practice (e.g. Amazon's two-person rule for AI-assisted changes); it's a sound norm.

assertions.quote: we're always talking about aggregating it on a team level. We're not ever talking about using it for individual performance management

verdicts.note: This is a management policy recommendation, not an empirical claim.

assertions.quote: AI is not a magic silver bullet

verdicts.note: The Stanford 100k-developer study and other field data put average gains around 10-20%, far below 2x-10x marketing claims.
